To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Akt1 activation inhibits invasion and metastasis of some cancer cells by inducing the ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of the transcription factor NFAT.
Akt1 activation in some cancer cells inhibits their invasion by promoting HDM2-mediated degradation of NFAT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of genes involved in the development and progression of cancer.
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of cancer cell invasion and metastasis and the development of novel anti-metastasis therapies.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that control the invasive phenotype of cancer cells and the development of therapeutic strategies to inhibit tumor metastasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Akt1 protein is not always a bad guy, and it is possible that Akt1 could have a role in the suppression of metastases.
Akt1 has both antimetastasis and metastatic functions.
Akt1 is a tumor suppressor in some cell types and a tumor promoter in others, but that it may also have a tumor suppressive role in the latter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Akt is a metastasis suppressors in certain cancer cell lines, and that this effect is mediated through HDM2-dependent degradation of NFATc2.
Akt1 has both oncogenic and anti-oncogenic functions.
the Akt signaling network can be used as a therapeutic target for the inhibition of cancer progression, but the use of this network to promote cancer cell death is not recommended.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Akt can be an invasion-suppressing factor in certain cancer types.
Akt1 can have a tumor-suppressive function in some cancer cells, and that this function can be mediated through HDM2 and NFAT.
Akt can have both pro- and antimetastasis activities in different cancer types and in the same cell type in response to different signals.
